beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about citations that nobody ever checks. Today we are going to learn why a reference pointing at nothing is more dangerous than no reference at all. My finance agent had been attaching evidence to every finding for weeks. Until this week, nothing had ever opened those files to see if the rows were there.

show.event: composer on cream; the fellow names himself and the subject
three output lines land, ending on the danger

props.command: The findings cite evidence. Has anything ever confirmed the cited rows exist?
output: Every finding already carried evidence references. That looked like proof.
Nothing had ever opened the files to confirm the rows were actually there.
A citation that points at nothing survives review because it looks like diligence.

beats.act: ACT 1 — THREE WAYS TO BE UNSOURCED
beats.narration_text: The word unsourced hides three different failures. A finding with no evidence at all. A reference naming a file that is not in the pack. And a reference to a file that exists, where the row it names does not. Only the first is visible by reading the report.

layers.title: UNCITED
layers.sub: no evidence attached at all; the only one visible by reading

layers.title: DANGLING
layers.sub: names a file that is not in the pack

layers.title: UNRESOLVED
layers.sub: the file is there; the row it points to is not

props.caption: The last two are what a citation check is actually for.

beats.act: ACT 1 — THREE WAYS TO BE UNSOURCED
beats.narration_text: Checking them starts with refusing to guess. A reference has a shape: file, column, value. If it does not parse, the engine raises rather than skipping it quietly, because a reference nobody can read is a defect in the finding, not noise to be tolerated on the way past.

show.event: the signature and docstring write on
the guard holds as the voice says 'does not parse'

props.title: coverage.py — refuse to guess

beats.narration_text: Then the actual work, which is unglamorous. Open the file the reference names. Read the column it names. Look for the value it names. If the row is there, the citation resolves. If it is not, say which of the three failures it was, rather than collapsing them into one word.

props.title: Open the File and Look
props.body: Read the column the reference names, look for the value it names. If the row is not there, say which failure it was rather than collapsing them.

beats.narration_text: Each failure reported on its own line. The first reference resolves. The second names a file that is not in this pack. The third names a file that is, with an account number that is not in it. And the fourth is a finding carrying nothing at all. Four different problems, four different answers.

props.artifactTitle: coverage — one reference at a time
artifactLines: ledger.csv:account=4000   ->  DANGLING    (file not in the pack)
budget.csv:account=9999   ->  UNRESOLVED  (file present, no such row)

beats.narration_text: So I ran it against the real February investigation, expecting to find something embarrassing. Twenty-one references across four findings. All twenty-one resolve. Every account number the agent cited is genuinely in the file it said it was in. That is the result I wanted and not the one I expected.

show.event: payroll completes the grid; caption settles

props.caption: Every cited row exists in the file the finding named.

beats.narration_text: A passing check is a weaker result than a failing one, and worth being honest about. It tells you the citations are not broken. It does not tell you the check works, because a check that always passes and a check that cannot fail look identical from the outside.

props.title: A Pass Proves Less Than a Fail
props.body: A check that always passes and a check that cannot fail look identical from outside. Passing tells you the citations are not broken, not that the check works.

beats.narration_text: Which is why each failure is tested separately against data built to break it. A file deleted. A row that does not exist. A column that does not exist. A finding stripped of evidence. Eleven cases, and the check is only worth its passing result because it demonstrably fails when it should.

show.event: the complete tally holds in terracotta

props.artifactTitle: the check must be able to fail
props.artifactHeading: Eleven cases, each built to break it
props.sparkLine: It can fail. So the pass counts.

beats.narration_text: The limit matters more than the result. Resolving a reference proves the row exists. It does not prove the row supports the claim. A finding can cite a real account, in a real file, and still be the wrong account entirely, and nothing here would notice.

show.event: 'A cited row' appears at the source
the three existence checks light in order
arc completes toward the unanswered question

props.destTitle: does this row actually support the claim?
props.arcCaption: three checks, none of them about meaning

beats.narration_text: And it reports rather than blocks. A report whose citations do not resolve still gets produced, with the problems listed. Making it a gate was the obvious next move and I did not take it, because I wanted to see how often this fires before letting it stop anything.

show.event: 'What it does not do' stacks on

props.sparkLine: It reports. It does not gate.

layers.title: What it does
layers.sub: lists every reference that did not resolve, and which failure it was

layers.title: What it does not do
layers.sub: stop the report being produced or sent

layers.title: Why not yet
layers.sub: a gate you have never watched fire is a gate you do not understand

props.caption: Deliberately a measurement first and a control later.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. Findings had been carrying evidence references for weeks, which looked like proof, and nothing had ever opened the files to check. The word unsourced hides three separate failures: no citation at all, a citation to a missing file, and a citation to a row that is not there. Each is now reported on its own, and a reference that cannot even be parsed raises rather than being skipped. Against the real February investigation all twenty-one references across four findings resolve. What that proves is that the rows exist. It does not prove they support the claims, and a perfectly resolving citation can still be the wrong account.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take something I generate that cites its sources, and for every citation tell me whether you could actually follow it to a specific row, file or line. Then separate the ones that are missing from the ones that merely look plausible. Run it on anything that produces references. The plausible-looking ones are the finding, because those are the citations that pass a review by looking right.

props.command: Take something I generate that cites its sources. For every citation, tell me whether you could follow it to a specific row, file or line. Then separate the ones that are missing from the ones that merely look plausible.
output: The plausible-looking citations are the finding. Those are the ones that pass review.
A reference nobody has followed is a claim, not a source.

beats.narration_text: That was evidence coverage for the Mycroft Finance Investigator. The code and the tests are in pull request seventeen. Adwait Changan, for Humanitarians AI.
